section_summary: This final section chiefly concerns Florida protests against scrap-iron shipments to Japan and the Roosevelt administration’s ensuing export-licensing and embargo policy. It also contains a warning relayed through Madrid that restrictions on essential supplies, especially gasoline, could lead to war. The last page shifts to a June 1941 assessment of Japan’s likely response to the German attack on the Soviet Union, including whether Japan might attack Siberia.

subfiles.title: Letter from Senator Charles O. Andrews forwarding protests against scrap-iron shipments
subfiles.about: Senator Andrews forwards two telegrams from Florida organizations protesting the loading of scrap iron for export.
subfiles.summary: Senator Andrews forwards two organizations' telegrams protesting scrap iron loading at a Florida port.

subfiles.title: Duplicate of Senator Andrews’s letter forwarding scrap-iron protests
subfiles.about: A duplicate copy records Andrews’s transmittal of two Florida protests against a scrap-iron shipment.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate of Andrews's October 4 letter forwarding two scrap-iron protest telegrams.

subfiles.title: Telegram from the Carl Vogel Unit protesting scrap-iron exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Helen McCoy, Secretary, Carl Vogel Unit Number 47, American Legion Auxiliary
subfiles.about: The American Legion Auxiliary unit at Lake Worth asks Andrews to oppose present and future scrap-iron shipments from Palm Beach to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Carl Vogel Unit 47 protests scrap-iron shipments from Palm Beach to Japan and asks Andrews's cooperation.

subfiles.title: Telegram from the Florida Federation of Labor protesting scrap-iron shipments
subfiles.from: Charles E. Silva, President, Florida Federation of Labor
subfiles.about: Silva asks Andrews to prevent scrap-iron cargoes from leaving several Florida ports for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Florida Federation of Labor protests scrap loading on a Greek steamer bound for Japan, with more at Fort Lauderdale, Jacksonville and Tampa.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull’s reply on United States scrap-iron export policy
subfiles.to: Charles O. Andrews, United States Senate
subfiles.about: Hull explains the President’s restrictions on exports of iron and steel scrap and returns the two Florida protest telegrams.
subfiles.summary: Hull says October 1 scrap licenses were cancelled and from October 16 licenses go only to the Western Hemisphere and Britain; encloses the release and customs instructions.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Madrid reporting a Japanese warning about embargo measures
subfiles.about: An unnamed Japanese naval attaché warns that continued American restrictions on essential exports to Japan would result in war.
subfiles.summary: Madrid telegram: the Japanese naval attaché warned his American counterpart on instructions that Japan must live and continued restrictions, especially on gasoline, would mean war.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Madrid telegram concerning Japanese reaction to embargoes
subfiles.about: This paraphrase restates the Japanese naval attaché’s warning that American export restrictions could produce war.
subfiles.summary: Paraphrase: the Japanese naval attaché in Madrid said continued American embargoes on essential materials, especially gasoline, would result in war.

subfiles.title: Transmittal memorandum on probable Japanese reactions to the German-Soviet war
subfiles.to: Unstated; copies to Mr. Hornbeck and Mr. Atherton
subfiles.about: The memorandum forwards two preliminary assessments of Japan’s likely response to war between Germany and the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Transmittal of two assessments of Japan's reaction to the German-Soviet war: Schmidt's most probable analysis, and Langdon's deterrents to attacking Siberia; both foresee uncertainty.
